Nurse
NURSE
n. and v.
From Old French nourice, from Latin nutrix, from nutrire, to nourish. Webster 1828: a woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own; one who tends the sick. Paul takes it up as an image of apostolic ministry.

Biblical Definition

Nurse in Scripture is a figure of tender, costly, unglamorous care, and Paul reaches for it to describe his own ministry. But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7) — and the Greek suggests a nursing mother with her own children, not a hired attendant; the next verse says the apostles were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls. Moses’ sister uses the office to reunite a rescued baby with his own mother: Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee? (Exodus 2:7) — and Pharaoh’s daughter pays Jochebed to raise her own son. Naomi, emptied at the start of the book, ends it holding a child: And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16). A nurse’s flight leaves a permanent mark in the royal house: his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). And Isaiah promises kings and queens as nursing fathers and nursing mothers to Zion (Isaiah 49:23).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NURSE as a woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own; a woman who tends the sick; and, as a verb, to nourish, to suckle, to tend in sickness, and figuratively to promote growth.

NURSE, n. — A woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own.

A woman who tends the sick; one who attends and cares for the helpless.

NURSE, v.t. — To suckle; to nourish at the breast; to tend, as an infant or a sick person.

Figuratively, to bring up, to foster, to promote the growth of anything — whence a nursery.

From Latin nutrix, from nutrio, to nourish — the root also of nutriment, nutrition, and nourish.

Key Scripture

1 Thessalonians 2:7 — "But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children:"

Exodus 2:7 — "Then said his sister to Pharaoh's daughter, Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee?"

Ruth 4:16 — "And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it."

2 Samuel 4:4 — "And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth."

Modern Corruption

1 Thessalonians 2:7 gives a nursing mother as the model for how a minister handles a congregation, which sits badly with both the executive model of pastoral leadership and the assumption that gentleness in a man is weakness.

expand to see more

Paul had every right to press his apostolic authority in Thessalonica and says so in the same breath — when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ — and then chooses the opposite: we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children. Three verses later he changes the figure to a father exhorting and charging his children, so the passage gives both, and neither is the executive. The dictionary holds male-only eldership without qualification; the office belongs to men. But the manner Scripture assigns to that office is nursing and fathering, not managing, and Peter forbids elders to be lords over God’s heritage. A man who cannot be gentle is not thereby more masculine; by this text he is less fit for the office.

The other three uses are worth holding together, because they show what such care costs and what it is worth. Jochebed nursed her own son for Pharaoh’s wages and gave him up again. Naomi, who had told the women of Bethlehem to call her Mara because the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her, ends the book with a child in her bosom and the neighbours saying there is a son born to Naomi — and that child is Obed, the grandfather of David. And Mephibosheth was lamed for life by a nurse running to save him, which is Scripture’s honest note that even faithful care in a crisis can leave permanent damage. The same lame man is later seated at David’s table continually, and the two facts are allowed to stand together.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yanaq (H3243), to suck, to nurse; omeneth (H539 participle), a nurse, one who supports; Greek trophos (G5162), a nurse; thalpo (G2282), to warm, to cherish.

expand to see more

Hebrew yanaq (H3243) — to suck, and in the causative to give suck; that she may nurse the child (Exodus 2:7).

Hebrew omeneth — a nurse, from aman, to support, be faithful; the same root as amen; became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16).

Greek trophos (G5162) — a nurse, a nursing mother; even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

Greek thalpo (G2282) — to warm, to cherish; the same verb used of a husband cherishing his wife (Ephesians 5:29).

Hebrew oman (H539) — a foster father, a nourisher; kings shall be thy nursing fathers (Isaiah 49:23).

Usage

"Even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7) — the manner Scripture assigns to the pastoral office."

"Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16) — the woman who called herself Mara, holding David’s grandfather."

"His nurse took him up, and fled… and he became lame (2 Samuel 4:4) — faithful care in a crisis, and permanent damage."
